2.text: St. Lawrence Island and to those of America, call themselves “Reindeer tribe”

3.text: (Čawčuwaˊt), meaning by this that they are nearer to the reindeer-herds than

4.text: “those of the other shore” (Roˊčhɪlɪt), and the name Aiˊwanat, given to them

5.text: by the inland reindeer-breeders, they apply in their turn to the people of the

6.text: other shore.¹ They give as a reason for this, that in their traffic with “those

7.text: of the other shore,” they offer the products of reindeer-breeding (reindeer-meat,

8.text: fawn-skins, ready-made clothes of reindeer-skin), while “those of the other

9.text: shore” bring the products of Maritime pursuits (seal-skins, thong, blubber).

10.text: Though this is quite true, still the contrast is much exaggerated.

11.text: One of the most frequent episodes of this tradition refers to a struggle

12.text: between a Čaˊwču warrior and a Maritime Aiˊwan. In the summer-time the

13.text: reindeer-breeder goes to the seashore, and finds there the Aiˊwan carving a

14.text: whale and hauling to the shore a quantity of walrus killed on a sea-hunt.

15.text: The reindeer-breeder is longing for the sea-meat. He visits the Aiˊwan, or

16.text: sends to him some member of his family, and asks for blubber. In some

17.text: versions the request is granted, and the Reindeer-man goes home peacefully

18.text: with the object of his desire. Thus, for instance, in the tale of “The Happy

19.text: Suitor,” the hero visits the Aiˊwan, and sees a walrus-carcass lying whole on

20.text: the ground. He says, “I come for blubber!” They answer, “Here is the

21.text: carcass: we will carve it, and cut a piece for you.” He says, “Better not

22.text: carve it. It is just a good carrying-load for my shoulder.” — “Oh, no! Will

23.text: you be able to carry it?” — “Oh, yes! if only you do not grudge it.” He

24.text: lifted the carcass on his shoulder and carried it home.²

25.text: Much more frequently, however, the Aiˊwan refuses the request. This

26.text: refusal is contrary to the customs of arctic life, which require liberality on the

27.text: part of a successful hunter, and, in case a whale has been captured, grant the

28.text: right to everyone to take part in the carving of the meat. So after the refusal

29.text: a wrestling-match ensues, in which the Reindeer-breeder vanquishes and kills

30.text: the Aiˊwan. Then he carries away the object of the strife. Thus, in the

31.text: third chapter of the tale of “Eleˊndi and His Sons,” two sons of Eleˊndi send

32.text: their old father to an Aiˊwan neighbor to ask for some whale-skin. The

33.text: Aiˊwan, in derision, fills with blubber the upper part of the old man’s breeches.

34.text: The young men get angry and run to the place. A whale’s carcass is lying

35.text: on the beach. The Aiˊwan’s working-people are busy carving whale-meat. The

36.text: two young men jump to the whale, and, raising their spears, drive away all the

37.text: people. The Aiˊwan calls to them, “Stop that! First kill me, then take my

38.text: whale!” But they pay no heed to his words. He says, “Bring the requisites

39.text: for a wrestling-match.” A walrus-hide is brought, and also some thigh-bones

40.text: of walrus. He spreads the hide upon the ground, breaks the bones into
